headline: Local tech worker creates 'Rent-A-Friend' profile, spends entire session explaining his own LinkedIn growth hacks to the hire
body:
Abhishek Nair, a 27-year-old product manager, officially became the city’s first 'professional friend' user to have his subscription revoked after he spent four consecutive hourly sessions pitching his 'Personal Brand Ecosystem' to his paid companion, Ramesh Kumar.

Kumar, who signed up for the platform expecting to engage in lighthearted banter or perhaps a movie outing, found himself instead being asked to endorse specific skills on Nair’s profile. 'I was hired to be a buddy, but for sixty minutes, I was effectively a human focus group for his upcoming newsletter launch,' Kumar stated. 'He kept asking if my engagement would increase if he used more bullet points in his morning reflections on perseverance.'

According to the platform’s terms of service, friends are meant to be 'neutral, supportive listeners,' not captive audiences for middle-management career advice. Nair, however, remains unbothered by the termination of his account. 'It’s a strategic pivot,' Nair explained. 'I’m now looking to hire a 'Professional Audience' to sit in on my Zoom calls and react appropriately when I make a joke about synergy, which is a much more scalable way to maintain social presence.'
caption: When the line between 'paid companion' and 'captive focus group' gets a little too blurry. Would you pay to have someone listen to your career updates? #RentAFriend #Networking #HustleCulture (satire)

It captures a vivid, relatable social disaster without falling into the nihilistic tone found in the other entries.
